2 Creating the AI Job Indicator
Following the same methodology established in the Data Cleaning section, jobs are classified as AI-related using keyword matching on title and skill fields.

ai_keywords_exact = [
    r"\bai\b", r"\bllm\b", r"\bmlops\b", r"\bnlp\b",
    r"\bml engineer\b", r"\btensorflow\b", r"\bpytorch\b"
]
ai_keywords_partial = [
    "artificial intelligence", "machine learning", "deep learning",
    "data scientist", "generative ai", "reinforcement learning",
    "computer vision", "large language model", "predictive modeling",
    "natural language processing", "neural network", "data science",
    "data engineer", "data analyst", "statistical modeling",
    "predictive analytics", "business intelligence"
]

def is_ai(title):
    t = str(title).lower()
    for kw in ai_keywords_exact:
        if re.search(kw, t): return 1
    for kw in ai_keywords_partial:
        if kw in t: return 1
    return 0

is_ai_udf = udf(is_ai, IntegerType())
sdf = sdf.withColumn("AI_JOB", is_ai_udf(col("TITLE_RAW")))
sdf.cache()

ai_counts = sdf.groupBy("AI_JOB").count().orderBy("AI_JOB").toPandas()
ai_counts.columns = ["AI Job", "Count"]
ai_counts["AI Job"] = ai_counts["AI Job"].map({0: "Non-AI", 1: "AI-Related"})
print(ai_counts)

       AI Job  Count
0      Non-AI  36731
1  AI-Related  14514



fig = px.pie(
    ai_counts,
    names="AI Job",
    values="Count",
    title="Distribution of AI vs. Non-AI Job Postings",
    color="AI Job",
    color_discrete_map={"AI-Related": "#e74c3c", "Non-AI": "#3498db"}
)
fig.update_layout(
    font=dict(family="Arial, sans-serif", size=13),
    title_font=dict(size=18),
    legend_title="Career Type"
)
fig.show()

                            
                                            


Insight: AI-related positions represent approximately 28% of all job postings in the dataset, capturing data science, analytics, business intelligence, and machine learning roles. This broader definition reflects the true scope of AI-adjacent careers in the 2024 labor market.

title: Predictive Modeling
text:
3 KMeans Clustering
KMeans clustering groups job postings based on occupational characteristics — experience requirements, education level, and SOC classification — to identify whether AI-related jobs form distinct natural clusters.
A data quality issue was identified during feature preparation: the MIN_EDULEVELS field uses the code 99 to mean “No Education Listed” — a missing-data flag rather than a true ordinal education level. Left uncorrected, this placeholder distorts distance-based clustering. We replace it with the median of valid education levels before clustering.

valid_edu = sdf.filter(col("MIN_EDULEVELS") != 99)
median_edu = valid_edu.approxQuantile("MIN_EDULEVELS", [0.5], 0.01)[0]
sdf = sdf.withColumn(
    "MIN_EDULEVELS_CLEAN",
    when(col("MIN_EDULEVELS") == 99, median_edu).otherwise(col("MIN_EDULEVELS"))
)
print(f"Median valid education level used for imputation: {median_edu}")

indexer_soc = StringIndexer(inputCol="SOC_2021_5", outputCol="SOC_ENC", handleInvalid="keep")
indexer_onet = StringIndexer(inputCol="ONET", outputCol="ONET_ENC", handleInvalid="keep")
sdf = indexer_soc.fit(sdf).transform(sdf)
sdf = indexer_onet.fit(sdf).transform(sdf)

cluster_features = ["MIN_YEARS_EXPERIENCE", "MIN_EDULEVELS_CLEAN", "SOC_ENC"]
assembler = VectorAssembler(inputCols=cluster_features, outputCol="features_raw")
sdf_vec = assembler.transform(sdf)

scaler = StandardScaler(inputCol="features_raw", outputCol="features", withMean=True, withStd=True)
scaler_model = scaler.fit(sdf_vec)
sdf_scaled = scaler_model.transform(sdf_vec).cache()

Median valid education level used for imputation: 2.0



3.1 Elbow Method and Silhouette Score
To determine the optimal number of clusters, we evaluate KMeans across k = 2 to 7 using both inertia (elbow method) and silhouette score.

evaluator = ClusteringEvaluator(featuresCol="features", predictionCol="prediction")
elbow_rows = []
for k in range(2, 8):
    km = KMeans(featuresCol="features", k=k, seed=42)
    model = km.fit(sdf_scaled)
    cost = model.summary.trainingCost
    preds = model.transform(sdf_scaled)
    sil = evaluator.evaluate(preds)
    elbow_rows.append({"k": k, "Inertia": cost, "Silhouette": sil})

elbow_df = pd.DataFrame(elbow_rows)
print(elbow_df)

   k       Inertia  Silhouette
0  2  61033.170034    0.835087
1  3  30113.318675    0.803789
2  4  25791.192762    0.743782
3  5  18840.199306    0.720179
4  6  13343.671097    0.795845
5  7  12028.902515    0.792499



fig = px.line(
    elbow_df, x="k", y="Inertia", markers=True,
    title="Elbow Method: Inertia vs. Number of Clusters",
    color_discrete_sequence=["#3498db"]
)
fig.update_layout(font=dict(family="Arial, sans-serif", size=13), title_font=dict(size=18), height=400)
fig.show()

                            
                                            



fig = px.line(
    elbow_df, x="k", y="Silhouette", markers=True,
    title="Silhouette Score vs. Number of Clusters",
    color_discrete_sequence=["#e74c3c"]
)
fig.update_layout(font=dict(family="Arial, sans-serif", size=13), title_font=dict(size=18), height=400)
fig.show()

                            
                                            


Insight: The elbow method shows the steepest drop in inertia between k=2 and k=3, after which the curve flattens substantially — the classic elbow point. While k=2 has the single highest silhouette score (0.835), k=3 retains a strong silhouette (0.804) while providing a richer, more interpretable three-way segmentation. k=3 is selected as the optimal number of clusters.

kmeans = KMeans(featuresCol="features", predictionCol="Cluster", k=3, seed=42)
kmeans_model = kmeans.fit(sdf_scaled)
sdf_clustered = kmeans_model.transform(sdf_scaled).cache()

cluster_profile = sdf_clustered.groupBy("Cluster").agg(
    avg("MIN_YEARS_EXPERIENCE").alias("Avg_Experience"),
    avg("MIN_EDULEVELS_CLEAN").alias("Avg_Education"),
    avg("AI_JOB").alias("Pct_AI")
).orderBy("Cluster").toPandas()

cluster_size = sdf_clustered.groupBy("Cluster").count().orderBy("Cluster").toPandas()
cluster_profile = cluster_profile.merge(cluster_size, on="Cluster")
print(cluster_profile)

   Cluster  Avg_Experience  Avg_Education    Pct_AI  count
0        0        4.327045       2.030315  0.317346  39386
1        1       10.180003       1.990579  0.109157   7961
2        2        4.370190       0.305028  0.293997   3898



plot_df = cluster_profile.copy()
plot_df["Cluster"] = plot_df["Cluster"].astype(str)

fig = px.bar(
    plot_df.sort_values("Cluster"),
    x="Cluster",
    y="count",
    title="Distribution of Job Clusters Identified by KMeans",
    labels={"Cluster": "Cluster ID", "count": "Number of Job Postings"},
    color="Cluster",
    color_discrete_sequence=px.colors.qualitative.Bold,
    category_orders={"Cluster": ["0", "1", "2"]}
)
fig.update_layout(
    font=dict(family="Arial, sans-serif", size=13),
    title_font=dict(size=18),
    showlegend=False,
    height=450
)
fig.show()

                            
                                            


Insight: Cluster 0 is the dominant group (76.9% of postings, ~4.3 years experience, ~Bachelor’s education). Cluster 1 represents senior/experienced roles (15.5%, ~10.2 years experience), and Cluster 2 represents lower-formal-education roles (7.6%, ~Associate’s or below). Experience — not education — is the primary axis separating these groups.

ai_cluster = sdf_clustered.groupBy("Cluster", "AI_JOB").count().toPandas()
ai_cluster["Type"] = ai_cluster["AI_JOB"].map({0: "Non-AI", 1: "AI-Related"})
ai_cluster["Cluster"] = ai_cluster["Cluster"].astype(str)

fig = px.bar(
    ai_cluster,
    x="Cluster",
    y="count",
    color="Type",
    barmode="stack",
    title="AI vs. Non-AI Distribution per Cluster",
    labels={"Cluster": "Cluster ID", "count": "Job Postings"},
    color_discrete_map={"AI-Related": "#e74c3c", "Non-AI": "#3498db"},
    category_orders={"Cluster": ["0", "1", "2"]}
)
fig.update_layout(
    font=dict(family="Arial, sans-serif", size=13),
    title_font=dict(size=18),
    height=450
)
fig.show()

                            
                                            


Insight: AI job density is highest in Cluster 0 (31.7%) and Cluster 2 (29.4%) — both lower-experience groups — but drops sharply in Cluster 1 (10.9%), the senior/high-experience group. This suggests AI-related roles skew toward earlier-career positions rather than senior traditional roles, regardless of formal education level.


3.2 PCA Visualization (Interactive)
To visualize the cluster structure in two dimensions, we project the scaled features onto their first two principal components. Use the dropdown below to toggle between coloring by Cluster or by AI Job Status.

pca = PCA(k=2, inputCol="features", outputCol="pca_features")
pca_model = pca.fit(sdf_clustered)
sdf_pca = pca_model.transform(sdf_clustered)

print(f"Explained variance (PC1, PC2): {pca_model.explainedVariance}")

pca_sample = sdf_pca.select("pca_features", "Cluster", "AI_JOB").sample(0.1, seed=42).toPandas()
pca_sample["PC1"] = pca_sample["pca_features"].apply(lambda v: float(v[0]))
pca_sample["PC2"] = pca_sample["pca_features"].apply(lambda v: float(v[1]))
pca_sample["Cluster"] = pca_sample["Cluster"].astype(str)
pca_sample["AI_Status"] = pca_sample["AI_JOB"].map({0: "Non-AI", 1: "AI-Related"})

cluster_colors = {"0": "#3498db", "1": "#e74c3c", "2": "#2ecc71"}
ai_colors = {"Non-AI": "#3498db", "AI-Related": "#e74c3c"}

fig = go.Figure()

cluster_ids = sorted(pca_sample["Cluster"].unique())
for c in cluster_ids:
    sub = pca_sample[pca_sample["Cluster"] == c]
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
        x=sub["PC1"], y=sub["PC2"], mode="markers",
        name=f"Cluster {c}",
        marker=dict(color=cluster_colors.get(c, "#888"), opacity=0.5, size=6),
        visible=True
    ))

for status in ["Non-AI", "AI-Related"]:
    sub = pca_sample[pca_sample["AI_Status"] == status]
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
        x=sub["PC1"], y=sub["PC2"], mode="markers",
        name=status,
        marker=dict(color=ai_colors[status], opacity=0.5, size=6),
        visible=False
    ))

n_cluster_traces = len(cluster_ids)
n_ai_traces = 2
cluster_visibility = [True]*n_cluster_traces + [False]*n_ai_traces
ai_visibility = [False]*n_cluster_traces + [True]*n_ai_traces

fig.update_layout(
    title="PCA Visualization — Colored by Cluster",
    xaxis_title="Overall Seniority Score (Experience + Education)",
    yaxis_title="Education-Experience Balance",
    font=dict(family="Arial, sans-serif", size=13),
    title_font=dict(size=18),
    height=520,
    updatemenus=[dict(
        type="dropdown",
        direction="down",
        x=1.0, xanchor="right",
        y=1.18, yanchor="top",
        buttons=[
            dict(label="Color by Cluster", method="update",
                 args=[{"visible": cluster_visibility},
                       {"title": "PCA Visualization — Colored by Cluster"}]),
            dict(label="Color by AI Job Status", method="update",
                 args=[{"visible": ai_visibility},
                       {"title": "PCA Visualization — Colored by AI Job Status"}]),
        ]
    )]
)
fig.show()

Explained variance (PC1, PC2): [0.5202318197128315,0.4797681802871685]


                            
                                            


Insight: The 2D PCA projection shows reasonably distinct groupings between clusters, confirming that the KMeans solution captures real structure in the data rather than arbitrary partitions. The grid-like point pattern reflects the discrete nature of experience and education values — relatively few unique combinations exist in the labor market, so many postings share identical coordinates. Switching the view to AI Job Status shows that AI-related postings are dispersed throughout the lower-experience region of the projection rather than forming their own isolated cluster — consistent with AI skills appearing across many traditional job categories rather than as a separate occupational class.

title: Predictive Modeling
text:
4 Classification Models
Two supervised models are trained to predict whether a job posting is AI-related, using experience, education, and occupational classification as features. Since AI-related jobs make up only ~28% of postings, class weights are computed and applied (equivalent to scikit-learn’s class_weight="balanced") to prevent the models from defaulting to the majority class.

features = ["MIN_YEARS_EXPERIENCE", "MIN_EDULEVELS_CLEAN", "SOC_ENC", "ONET_ENC"]
assembler2 = VectorAssembler(inputCols=features, outputCol="features_raw2")
sdf_feat = assembler2.transform(sdf_clustered)

scaler2 = StandardScaler(inputCol="features_raw2", outputCol="features_scaled2", withMean=True, withStd=True)
scaler2_model = scaler2.fit(sdf_feat)
sdf_feat_scaled = scaler2_model.transform(sdf_feat)

train_df, test_df = sdf_feat_scaled.randomSplit([0.8, 0.2], seed=42)

counts = {row["AI_JOB"]: row["count"] for row in train_df.groupBy("AI_JOB").count().collect()}
total = sum(counts.values())
w0 = total / (2 * counts[0])
w1 = total / (2 * counts[1])
train_df = train_df.withColumn("weight", when(col("AI_JOB") == 1, w1).otherwise(w0))
print(f"Class weights -> Non-AI: {w0:.3f}, AI-Related: {w1:.3f}")

lr = LogisticRegression(featuresCol="features_scaled2", labelCol="AI_JOB", weightCol="weight", maxIter=1000)
lr_model = lr.fit(train_df)
lr_pred = lr_model.transform(test_df).select("AI_JOB", "prediction").toPandas()

rf = RandomForestClassifier(featuresCol="features_raw2", labelCol="AI_JOB", weightCol="weight", numTrees=100, seed=42)
rf_model = rf.fit(train_df)
rf_pred = rf_model.transform(test_df).select("AI_JOB", "prediction").toPandas()

print("\n=== Logistic Regression ===")
print(f"Accuracy: {accuracy_score(lr_pred['AI_JOB'], lr_pred['prediction']):.4f}")
print(f"F1 Score: {f1_score(lr_pred['AI_JOB'], lr_pred['prediction']):.4f}")
print("\n=== Random Forest ===")
print(f"Accuracy: {accuracy_score(rf_pred['AI_JOB'], rf_pred['prediction']):.4f}")
print(f"F1 Score: {f1_score(rf_pred['AI_JOB'], rf_pred['prediction']):.4f}")

F1 Score: 0.4254

Accuracy: 0.6774

    "Logistic Regression": confusion_matrix(lr_pred['AI_JOB'], lr_pred['prediction']),
    "Random Forest": confusion_matrix(rf_pred['AI_JOB'], rf_pred['prediction'])
}

for model_name, cm in results.items():
    fig = px.imshow(
        cm,
        text_auto=True,
        labels=dict(x="Predicted", y="Actual", color="Count"),
        x=["Non-AI", "AI-Related"],

        color_continuous_scale="Blues"

Insight: With balanced class weights and corrected education data, both models achieve ~67% accuracy and F1 scores around 0.43. Random Forest slightly outperforms Logistic Regression, suggesting modest nonlinear relationships in the data. The improvement over the uncorrected education feature confirms that fixing the placeholder values produced a cleaner, more reliable signal.

importance_df = pd.DataFrame({

print(importance_df)

Insight: Years of experience is overwhelmingly the strongest predictor of AI job classification (importance: 0.885), with education contributing a much smaller share (0.115). Occupational classification codes (SOC, ONET) contribute almost nothing once experience and education are accounted for — reinforcing the clustering finding that career stage, not job title taxonomy, differentiates AI roles.

Even accounting for this, postings with at least a Bachelor’s degree show meaningfully higher AI density than those requiring only a high school diploma or equivalent.

title: Predictive Modeling
text:
5 Summary
This ML analysis extends the EDA by applying PySpark MLlib clustering and classification models to the AI vs. Non-AI career question.
Key findings:

AI-related jobs represent approximately 28% of postings after filtering invalid placeholder records, confirming that AI has broadly permeated the labor market beyond a narrow technical niche
A data quality issue was identified and corrected: the education field used code 99 as a “missing data” flag, which was distorting both clustering and classification results
The elbow method and silhouette score jointly support k=3 as the optimal number of clusters, yielding interpretable groups differentiated primarily by years of experience
AI job density is highest among lower-experience clusters (~30%) and lowest among senior/high-experience roles (10.9%), suggesting AI roles concentrate earlier in career trajectories
Logistic Regression and Random Forest achieve ~67% accuracy and F1 scores of ~0.43 after correcting the education feature and applying balanced class weights
Years of experience is by far the dominant predictor of AI job classification (88.5% importance), far outweighing education (11.5%) and occupational codes (~0%)

Recommendations for job seekers:

Early-to-mid career professionals are well-positioned to enter AI-adjacent roles, since AI job density is highest in lower-experience clusters
Formal education level matters less than expected — occupational and skills alignment appear more important than degree level alone
Build demonstrable experience with data science, analytics, or ML tools early in one’s career, since experience — not credentials — is the strongest signal in this analysis
Target industries like Professional Services, Finance, and Information Technology where AI hiring is most concentrated

title: Project Overview
text:
Research Question

How does AI impact job security, salary, and career growth across industries in 2024?

Specifically, we investigate:

Which industries are experiencing AI-driven job growth vs. job displacement?
How do salaries compare between AI and non-AI careers?
What skills differentiate AI roles from traditional ones?
Are new job titles emerging due to AI advancements?

title: Project Overview
text:
Research Rationale
Our group shall focus on the research topic “AI vs Non-AI Careers”, given the implementation of AI across industrial sectors remains one of the most relevant forces for either future job growth or displacement. Although AI has existed even before 2020, when it first began its adoption into society at large, only in the past few years and especially since 2024 has the job market been so vividly influenced by its implementation. Jobs have been completely automated and some new ones created, applications to those jobs streamlined under AI overview rather than Human, and industries of all varieties have seen some form of AI implementation, or at least the pressure to adopt it. While other economic factors have contributed to it, the human element behind how AI influences job security, displacement, creation, and otherwise is what our group finds most vital for future analysis.
As such, our group aims to answer how AI impacts job security, which industries are experiencing AI-driven job growth and which job displacement, how do AI-powered careers compare to traditional roles, and are new job titles emerging due to AI advancements alongside these displacements. These aspects reflect the duality of AI, and how universal it has been across industries, rather than limited to a select few and possibly only looking at the negatives. 2024 specifically was reported to have had 23–27% of employees in the U.S. admit to having used AI in their work at least once during the past week, and then about 9–10% claimed they used it every day at work (Bick et al., 2024). Such prevalence of AI, as we hope to find, will tell what the potential future ratio of AI job creation and displacement, and net influences of AI across industries will be. From this, a better grasp of future economic conditions and trends can be found.

title: Project Overview
text:
Literature Review
Looking at previous scholarly works, there has already been much research into the impacts of AI across industries in recent years, both positive and negative. To start, based on correlations between AI exposure and stress, anxiety, and burnout within jobs, it was found the implementation of AI to even minor degrees will correlate very strongly with increased job insecurity (Hassan & Anwer, 2024). Instantly, it is clear AI has heavily disrupted current industries and the security which their workers feel, even when not directly threatened with replacement by said AI. The very idea of AI being in the workplace is enough to cause unease, and thus lead to perhaps irrational acts of defense by employees against these models. This isn’t entirely unfounded, however, as more repetitive roles such as communications manager, data entry, mail clerk, and data collector all face the possibility of around 92-98% AI replacement. On the other hand, more complex jobs such as that of a hospitalist, immunologist, physician, and mental health clinician only face around 10% AI replacement, a far cry from the past examples (Balakumar et al., 2024). This displays how while some industries and careers are more prone to AI encroachment, others still remain relatively stable against such displacement. #Data Cleaning & Preprocessing We have removed multiple versions of NAICS and SOC codes because they represent classifications of the same industries and occupations at different levels of detail. For example, NAICS2, NAICS3, NAICS4, NAICS5, and NAICS6 belong to the same industry classification hierarchy, while SOC_2, SOC_3, SOC_4, and SOC_5 belong to the same occupational classification hierarchy. Retaining all levels would result in redundant information and unnecessarily complicate the dataset. Therefore, we will retain one classification level and remove the remaining versions to simplify the dataset, reduce duplication, and improve analytical efficiency. What is worth mentioning, though, is the type of industry, based on metrics such as traditionalism or modernism, is mostly irrelevant to being susceptible to AI encroachment. Even “old school” industries, like farming, see AI implementation in processes like the irrigation of crops, where now models can better analyze the optimal output of water for crops based on certain environmental conditions (Onteddu et al., 2024). So while any industry is capable of being reshaped by AI, the question largely remains whether it will be a net positive or negative. As of now, estimations call for roughly 83 million jobs that are expected to be displaced as a result of AI by 2030, whereas approximately 69 million jobs are to be created for the same reason (Singh, 2025). In terms of this estimate, at least, AI is set to create more displacement than opportunity, yet the full scope of AI’s place in the industry job market is not fully understood, so there is much left to be researched. Overall, though, one cannot deny the impact which AI has had and continues to have on jobs across all economic industries.

text:
5 Summary
This exploratory analysis looked at AI-related and non-AI careers in the 2024 Lightcast job postings dataset. Since the dataset does not already label whether a job is AI-related, a rule-based indicator was created using AI and machine learning terms found in the job title and skill fields. With this approach, the dataset includes 7,524 AI-related postings and 61,674 non-AI postings.
The career area analysis shows that AI-related postings are much smaller in number than non-AI postings, but they still appear across several fields, including Information Technology and Computer Science, Business Management and Operations, Healthcare, and Marketing and Public Relations. The industry analysis shows that AI-related postings are concentrated in industries such as Professional, Scientific, and Technical Services, Finance and Insurance, Manufacturing, Information, Educational Services, Retail Trade, and Health Care and Social Assistance.
The skills analysis shows that AI-related jobs often require a combination of technical and business-oriented skills, such as SQL, Python, Data Analysis, Machine Learning, Artificial Intelligence, Data Science, Tableau, AWS, Microsoft Azure, Business Intelligence, Power BI, Data Visualization, and Communication. Overall, the EDA suggests that AI-related career opportunities are connected not only to specialized AI roles, but also to broader data, technology, business, and service-related work.

title: KMeans clustering was used to identify natural groupings of job postings based on occupational characteristics. The goal was to determine whether AI-related jobs form distinct clusters compared to traditional occupations. By grouping similar jobs together without predefined labels, clustering helps reveal patterns in education requirements, experience requirements, and occupational classifications that may be associated with AI-driven careers. The KMeans model used the following features, SOC_ENC (encoded Standard Occupational Classification code), and ONET_ENC (encoded ONET occupation code). These variables represent occupational categories and job classifications used throughout the labor market. They were selected because the project instructions specifically recommend using SOC, NAICS, or O*NET classifications for clustering analysis. The clustering results suggest that the labor market can be segmented into distinct occupational groups. AI-related jobs appear to occupy specific occupational categories rather than being evenly distributed across all professions. For job seekers, this indicates that transitioning into AI-related work may be easier from occupations that already belong to technology-oriented or analytical occupational clusters than from occupations with little overlap in required skills.

title: Career Strategy
text:
Our analysis suggests that AI is not replacing the entire job market in a simple or uniform way. Instead, AI-related opportunities appear to be concentrated in certain career areas, industries, and skill profiles. For job seekers, this means the best strategy is not only to become an AI specialist, but to build a flexible career profile that combines domain knowledge, data skills, technical tools, and communication skills.
The literature review shows that AI has created both opportunity and uncertainty in the labor market. Prior research suggests that workers often experience higher job insecurity when AI is introduced into the workplace, especially in roles that involve repetitive or automatable tasks. At the same time, more complex and human-centered roles appear less vulnerable to full replacement. This supports the idea that job seekers should focus on building skills that are difficult to automate, while also learning how to use AI and data tools productively.
Our EDA supports this view. In the 2024 Lightcast job postings dataset, AI-related postings made up a smaller share of the total job postings, but they appeared across several major career areas. AI-related demand was especially visible in Information Technology and Computer Science, Business Management and Operations, Healthcare, and Marketing and Public Relations. At the industry level, AI-related postings were concentrated in Professional, Scientific, and Technical Services, Finance and Insurance, Manufacturing, Information, Educational Services, Retail Trade, and Health Care and Social Assistance. This suggests that AI career opportunities are not limited to traditional technical roles. Instead, AI is becoming relevant across business, healthcare, finance, education, and service-related industries.
The skill gap analysis also shows that AI-related career preparation requires a combination of technical and professional skills. The most important areas for improvement are Python, SQL, machine learning, artificial intelligence, cloud computing, and applied data analysis. However, communication also remains important because many AI-related roles require translating technical findings into business decisions. Therefore, job seekers should not only focus on coding or AI tools, but also on explaining insights clearly and applying them to real organizational problems.
The predictive modeling results further support this career strategy. The clustering and classification models suggest that AI-related jobs are more common in lower-experience and early-to-mid career clusters than in senior or high-experience roles. Years of experience was also the strongest predictor in the classification model, while education level was less important than expected after correcting the missing-value issue in the education field. This suggests that job seekers may benefit from building applied AI and analytics experience early, rather than relying only on formal credentials.

text:
2 Recommendations for Job Seekers

2.1 Build AI-adjacent skills, not only AI-specialist skills
Job seekers should develop skills that connect AI to practical business use cases. The EDA and skill gap analysis show strong demand for SQL, Python, data analysis, machine learning, artificial intelligence, Tableau, AWS, Microsoft Azure, Power BI, data visualization, and communication. These skills are useful not only for AI engineer roles, but also for business analyst, data analyst, product analyst, operations analyst, and strategy roles that increasingly use AI-supported tools.


2.2 Target industries where AI hiring is already visible
AI-related hiring appears more concentrated in Professional, Scientific, and Technical Services, Finance and Insurance, Manufacturing, Information, Educational Services, Retail Trade, and Health Care and Social Assistance. Job seekers interested in AI-related roles should prioritize these industries because they show stronger evidence of AI-related demand in the dataset. This does not mean other industries are irrelevant, but these sectors may offer more accessible entry points for AI-adjacent career development.


2.3 Use early-career experience strategically
The predictive modeling results suggest that AI-related roles are more common in lower-experience clusters. This is important for students and early-to-mid career professionals because it means AI-related opportunities may be accessible before reaching senior-level experience. Job seekers should focus on internships, class projects, portfolio projects, certifications, and applied analytics work that demonstrate practical experience with AI, machine learning, and data tools.


2.4 Avoid roles that rely only on repetitive tasks
The literature review suggests that repetitive and highly automatable roles face greater risk from AI displacement. Therefore, job seekers should avoid positioning themselves only around routine data entry, basic reporting, or task execution. Instead, they should build skills in problem-solving, interpretation, stakeholder communication, and decision support. These abilities are harder to automate and make technical skills more valuable.


2.5 Combine technical skills with domain knowledge
AI-related jobs are spread across multiple industries, which means domain knowledge still matters. For example, AI in finance, healthcare, manufacturing, education, and retail may require different business problems, regulations, data types, and stakeholder needs. Job seekers can stand out by combining technical skills with industry-specific knowledge rather than presenting themselves as general AI users only.


2.6 Create evidence of applied ability
Because the modeling results suggest that experience is a stronger signal than education level alone, job seekers should create concrete evidence of their skills. This can include GitHub projects, dashboards, machine learning notebooks, cloud-based analytics projects, or case studies. A strong portfolio can help show that the candidate can apply AI and data tools to real problems, not just list the tools on a resume.

3 Conclusion
Overall, our findings suggest that the strongest career strategy is to become AI-adjacent, data-capable, and industry-aware. AI-related jobs are still a smaller portion of the overall job market, but they are visible across many industries and career areas. Job seekers who combine technical skills, business communication, and applied project experience will be better positioned for both AI-specific and non-AI roles as the labor market continues to change.

title: AI vs. Non-AI Careers
text:
#Research Rationale Our group shall focus on the research topic “AI vs Non-AI Careers”, given the implementation of AI across industrial sectors remains one of the most relevant forces for either future job growth or displacement. Although AI has existed even before 2020, when it first began its adoption into society at large, only in the past few years and especially since 2024 has the job market been so vividly influenced by its implementation. Jobs have been completely automated and some new ones created, applications to those jobs streamlined under AI overview rather than Human, and industries of all varieties have seen some form of AI implementation, or at least the pressure to adopt it. While other economic factors have contributed to it, the human element behind how AI influences job security, displacement, creation, and otherwise is what our group finds most vital for future analysis.
As such, our group aims to answer how AI impacts job security, which industries are experiencing AI-driven job growth and which job displacement, how do AI-powered careers compare to traditional roles, and are new job titles emerging due to AI advancements alongside these displacements. These aspects reflect the duality of AI, and how universal it has been across industries, rather than limited to a select few and possibly only looking at the negatives. 2024 specifically was reported to have had 23–27% of employees in the U.S. admit to having used AI in their work at least once during the past week, and then about 9–10% claimed they used it every day at work (Bick et al., 2024). Such prevalence of AI, as we hope to find, will tell what the potential future ratio of AI job creation and displacement, and net influences of AI across industries will be. From this, a better grasp of future economic conditions and trends can be found.
#Literature Review Looking at previous scholarly works, there has already been much research into the impacts of AI across industries in recent years, both positive and negative. To start, based on correlations between AI exposure and stress, anxiety, and burnout within jobs, it was found the implementation of AI to even minor degrees will correlate very strongly with increased job insecurity (Hassan & Anwer, 2024). Instantly, it is clear AI has heavily disrupted current industries and the security which their workers feel, even when not directly threatened with replacement by said AI. The very idea of AI being in the workplace is enough to cause unease, and thus lead to perhaps irrational acts of defense by employees against these models. This isn’t entirely unfounded, however, as more repetitive roles such as communications manager, data entry, mail clerk, and data collector all face the possibility of around 92-98% AI replacement. On the other hand, more complex jobs such as that of a hospitalist, immunologist, physician, and mental health clinician only face around 10% AI replacement, a far cry from the past examples (Balakumar et al., 2024). This displays how while some industries and careers are more prone to AI encroachment, others still remain relatively stable against such displacement. #Data Cleaning & Preprocessing We have removed multiple versions of NAICS and SOC codes because they represent classifications of the same industries and occupations at different levels of detail. For example, NAICS2, NAICS3, NAICS4, NAICS5, and NAICS6 belong to the same industry classification hierarchy, while SOC_2, SOC_3, SOC_4, and SOC_5 belong to the same occupational classification hierarchy. Retaining all levels would result in redundant information and unnecessarily complicate the dataset. Therefore, we will retain one classification level and remove the remaining versions to simplify the dataset, reduce duplication, and improve analytical efficiency. What is worth mentioning, though, is the type of industry, based on metrics such as traditionalism or modernism, is mostly irrelevant to being susceptible to AI encroachment. Even “old school” industries, like farming, see AI implementation in processes like the irrigation of crops, where now models can better analyze the optimal output of water for crops based on certain environmental conditions (Onteddu et al., 2024). So while any industry is capable of being reshaped by AI, the question largely remains whether it will be a net positive or negative. As of now, estimations call for roughly 83 million jobs that are expected to be displaced as a result of AI by 2030, whereas approximately 69 million jobs are to be created for the same reason (Singh, 2025). In terms of this estimate, at least, AI is set to create more displacement than opportunity, yet the full scope of AI’s place in the industry job market is not fully understood, so there is much left to be researched. Overall, though, one cannot deny the impact which AI has had and continues to have on jobs across all economic industries.
